3.0.s.en: 1. He curses the day of his birth and wishes he had not been born

3.0.0.en: 1 After this Job opened his mouth, and cursed his day. 2 And Job spake, and said: 3 Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said, There is a man child conceived. 4 Let that day be darkness; let not God regard it from above, neither let day shine upon it. 5 Let darkness and the shadow of death rule over it; let a cloud dwell upon it; let the blackness of the day terrify it. 6 As for that night, let darkness seize upon it; let it not rejoice among the days of the year, let it not come into the number of the months. 7 Lo, let that night be barren, let no shout be heard in it. 8 Let them curse it that curse the day, who are ready to rouse up the dragon. 9 Let the stars of the evening thereof be dark; let it look for light, but have none; neither let it see the eyelashes of the morning: 10 Because it shut not up the doors of my mother's womb, nor hid sorrow from mine eyes.

3.0.1.en: It was a weakness in his life that Job cursed his conception. Although he is described as upright, he cursed his day, yet he did not blaspheme against God.

3.0.2.en: After this Job opened his mouth, and Job cursed his day. [1]

3.0.3.en: Ezekiel sat in the land of captivity, and his soul was groaning because of the destruction and ruin to which the people and their city and the temple had come. He was silent seven days, astonished, and the word of the LORD came to him (Ezek 3:15-16). And Job sat among his friends, and his soul was groaning over what had befallen him, so he opened his mouth after the long silence to curse the day of his conception and the day of his birth and the days of his trial.

3.0.4.en: Both were silent, Ezekiel and Job. The first was occupied with what belongs to God and His people and His temple and His city, and the second with what concerns himself and what people think of him. The first enjoyed the surpassing word of God, and the second descended to despair and bitterness and cursed his life.

3.0.5.en: We need to sit in silence, but to rise above the ego, to be occupied with what belongs to God and people and not with ourselves and our dignity. Then the Holy Spirit of God lifts us up as if to heaven, and we hear the divine voice and discover the divine mysteries that grant living hope.

3.0.6.en: Sadly, Job looked at the day of his conception as the worst day in history, and reckoned it the starting point of his unbearable sufferings. He forgot the good things he had enjoyed. The lean years devoured the years filled with blessings. His mind became a prisoner of the bitterness in which he lives, so he looked at his whole life through an extremely gloomy lens.

3.0.7.en: What befell Job befalls many when their days of affliction are prolonged. So we hear the prophet Jeremiah cry out: “Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me” (Jer 15:10); “Cursed be the day wherein I was born” (Jer 20:14).

3.0.8.en: When the day of our eternal meeting with our Christ on the clouds is hidden from our eyes even for moments, the world grows narrow upon us and we even reckon our creation to be in vain. [How long, LORD? wilt thou hide thyself for ever?... wherefore hast thou made all men in vain?] (Ps 89:46-47).

3.0.9.en: Here we pause a little before mankind's concern with birthday celebrations since ancient times. We find the wicked finding in this day the opportunity to express what is in their hearts of frivolity and earnest desire to dominate others, while the children of God stand in seriousness looking at their entering the path of sufferings. They reckon the day of their birth to be the day of their entering the valley of tears, but in a living, joyful hope that they are passing over to the new heavenly life.

3.0.10.en: * At birthday celebrations, where the desire for the domineering word rules over (the wicked), they dance to express by the movements of their bodies this word.

3.0.11.en: Someone noticed that the Book of Genesis speaks of Pharaoh's birthday (Gen 40:20), where it is said that the unruly man loves matters concerning birthdays. I have taken this quotation from him, for I have not found in the Holy Scripture any righteous man who made a birthday for himself. Herod was more unjust than this famous Pharaoh. For the latter killed the chief baker at the celebration of his birthday, while the former killed John.

3.0.12.en: Origen Origen expounded at length in his comment on the words of the prophet Jeremiah: “Woe is me, my mother, that thou hast borne me a man of strife” (Jer 15:10), which I have presented previously in the commentary on the Book of Jeremiah. Here I quote short passages:

3.0.13.en: * Who am I, that I was born only to be condemned, and to be quarreled with by men because of my reproof and blame of them, and because of my teachings which I teach to all the inhabitants of the earth.

3.0.14.en: Origen Truly, whoever has experienced the day of his second birth by water and the Spirit and has become a son of God does not curse even the day of his bodily birth, reckoning all his sufferings a crucifixion and burial with his Christ, and a narrow way by which he enters the open gates of heaven and the joy of the eternal resurrection.

3.0.15.en: Here we must not deny that despite the bitterness Job reached to the point of cursing the day of his conception, he did not blaspheme against God, nor did he regret his worship of Him. What he uttered reveals the bitterness of his soul, but he submitted to the will of God. He is under sufferings like us!

3.0.16.en: * What is understood by “After this”? After the arrival of his friends... for those who drew near did not greet him as a wrestler and did not ask him: How are you? They offered no remedies for the sores, nor did they stand upon the price Job had won for his treasure of virtues. They did not say to him: Do not lose heart, for your comforter is near you; do not fear, for your enemy is being defeated. Do not be ashamed, for the end is not far, and the victory is at the doors.

3.0.17.en: * “Let the day perish wherein I was born,” not the day on which he was created, but on which he was born... For God created me in goodness, but Eve who disobeyed bore me in troubles (Gen 3:16). David was not ignorant of this, but understood by the Spirit and said in a prophetic psalm: [In iniquities my mother conceived me, and in sin she bore me] (Ps 51:5).

3.0.18.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * O wonder that truly surpasses nature! Astounding events!

3.0.19.en: Death, once hated and execrated, is now surrounded with praises and considered blessed! After it used to bring mourning and grief and tears and dismal gloom, behold, it has appeared as a cause of joy and the center of a festive celebration!

3.0.20.en: For all the servants of God their death is declared a joy! For the end of their life alone gives them the assurance that they were received by God. Therefore their death is called blessed, because it seals their perfection and shows their blessedness, since the steadfastness of virtue prevails over them, as the saying of Inspiration: [Call no man happy before his death] (Sir 11:30). We do not apply this saying to you (O Mary), because your blessedness does not come from death, and your death did not complete your perfection... Not at your death, but from this very conception you are called blessed by all generations. No, it is never death that made you blessed, but you cast death down and dispelled its gloom and showed that it is joy (in Christ, born of you).

3.0.21.en: Fr. John of Damascus *Is it not shameful that you groan because of death, while Paul sighs because of the present life, writing to the Romans: [The whole creation groaneth and travaileth in pain together... but ourselves also, which have the firstfruits of the Spirit, even we ourselves groan within ourselves] (Rom 8:22-23). He says this not to condemn present things, but out of longing for the things to come.

3.1.0.en: St. John Chrysostom And Job spake, and said: [2]

3.1.1.en: St. John Chrysostom sees that the friends' silence throughout the week reveals the dreadfulness of what had happened, and that they were unable to utter a word unless he began first to speak.

3.1.2.en: Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said,

3.2.0.en: There is a man child conceived! [3]

3.2.1.en: Most likely Job was a king or a chief, and the day of his birth was a day the people prized, so he wished that this day be blotted out and cast into the sea of oblivion, where it becomes a sight of misery and wretchedness.

3.2.2.en: * Job knew that his birth was the beginning of all woes, so he longed that the day on which he was born would perish so that the root of all troubles might be removed. He desired that the day of his birth perish in order to receive the day of the resurrection. Solomon heard the saying of his father: “LORD, make me to know mine end, and the measure of my days, what it is: that I may know how frail I am” (Ps 39:4). For David knew that what is perfect cannot be possessed here, therefore he was hastening toward the things to come. Now we know in part, but it will be possible to attain perfection when the truth, not the shadow, of the divine and eternal majesty begins to shine, and we see it with open face (1 Cor 13:12; 2 Cor 3:18).

3.2.3.en: * Bodily pleasure and enjoyment in this life have drawn us, and we have come to fear to complete this journey in which there will be more bitterness than pleasure. But the saints and the wise lamented the length of life in this journey, since they reckoned departure to be with Christ far more glorious (Phil 1:23). They did not curse the day of their birth as one of them did: “Let the day perish wherein I was born” (Job 3:3).

3.2.4.en: St. Ambrose * This is also what the Preacher (Ecclesiastes) said: “Wherefore I praised the dead which are already dead more than the living which are yet alive” (Eccl 4:2)...

3.2.5.en: These are words that announce a disheartened and deeply affected soul. For David also says: “I said in my consternation (my great fear)...” (Ps 31:22)... and in another passage: “And I said in my tranquility, I shall never be moved” (Ps 30:6). This is also what Job said in his sorrow. Do you not see, my beloved, that those who are hurt utter loud cries? Do you blame them? No, rather we excuse them! For if they did not express themselves in this way, it would seem as though they did not share in human nature. Do you not hear Moses say: “If thou deal thus with me, kill me, I pray thee, out of hand” (Num 11:15)...

3.2.6.en: Do not listen to the bare words, but search for the basis of the thought. You have heard that Job “did not sin... with his lips” (Job 2:10), and he did not sin even after he uttered those words. Behold, you hear God Himself saying again: “Do you think that I deal with you in any other way than to declare your righteousness?” (Job 40:3) LXX.

3.2.7.en: St. John Chrysostom * Perhaps you say that God is the creator and builder of the world (Heb 11:10) [so why do we not love the world?]

3.2.8.en: You speak truly. But the bearers of God despise the world, not the world that God created from the elements and that He fashioned, but the one we made by our conduct, a different, corrupt world, of which the deceiving enemy has been made the prince by us (Jn 12:31; 14:30; 16:11).

3.2.9.en: This is what the Lord affirms precisely, for He said this to His disciples: “the prince of this world cometh, and hath nothing in me” (Jn 14:30). It is not without reason that He says: “prince of this world,” but He said so lest you think He is speaking of this visible creation, for our enemy is not the prince of this world, and the traitor has no power at all over the elements.

3.2.10.en: In what sense does He say: “the prince of this world cometh,” except the world that we make not according to the will of God, and by which we give a basis for unbelief and disobedience and disorder and every kind of sins?

3.2.11.en: To this world Paul clearly refers in accordance with the word of the Lord, saying in his Epistle to the Ephesians: “And you who were dead in trespasses and sins, wherein in time past ye walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit that now worketh in the children of disobedience” (Eph 2:1-2). Thus we have formed an evil world, and in this world we have made ourselves self-sufficient, needing no others, from corrupt sources...

3.2.12.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Let him say: “Let the day perish wherein I was born, and the night in which it was said... There is a man child conceived” [3], as though he said: Let the delight that hastens man to sin perish, and the weakness of his unrestrained mind, by which he becomes blind like one who has reached the darkness that consents to evil.

3.3.0.en: Let not God regard it from above, neither let the day shine upon it [4].

3.3.1.en: He wished that the day of his birth had been darkness, because the light of his life had been extinguished and the sun had set upon him, and perhaps he wanted his whole life to be night, so that he would sleep and not rise.

3.3.2.en: Despite the godliness and uprightness and faith Job reached, the Book does not hide his human weaknesses, so we do not marvel if thoughts of despair passed through him, wishing he had not been born. The Fathers have warned us of the wrong fear that leads to despair.

3.3.3.en: * There is a contrition of heart that is spiritual and useful, and this touches the heart in its depths. And there is another contrition, harmful and disturbing, which leads it only to defeat (like despair).

3.3.4.en: St. Mark the Ascetic * If labor (in keeping good thoughts) wears us out, we fall into despair; therefore may we hasten to the rock of knowledge and recite the Psalms and know the virtues upon the strings of the harp of knowledge.

3.3.5.en: Fr. Evagrius the monk Let darkness and the shadow of death rule over it.

3.3.6.en: Let a cloud dwell upon it.

3.4.0.en: Let the blackness (darkness) of the day terrify it [5].

3.4.1.en: * “Let darkness and the shadow of death rule over it,” since darkness is truly our enemy, just as Christ is the light (Jn 8:12; 9:5; 12:46). For this very reason (the traitor) is darkness.

3.4.2.en: And as Christ is righteousness (1 Cor 1:30), so (the traitor) is sin.

3.4.3.en: And as He is the source of life (Ps 36:9) and the image of His substance, so the traitor is “the shadow of death” (Heb 2:14-15).

3.4.4.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem * Is there anything more terrifying than Satan? Yes, for in resisting him we find no shield except faith (1 Pet 5:9), for it is a hidden shield against an unseen enemy, who shoots various arrows in the darkness of night (Ps 11:2) at the unwatchful. Since we have an unseen enemy we need faith as a mighty weapon of war, as the Apostle says: “Above all, taking the shield of faith, wherewith ye shall be able to quench all the fiery darts of the wicked” (Eph 6:16). So when the devil aims the arrow of fiery, impure lust, faith presents the image of judgment, so the mind cools and the arrow is quenched.

3.5.0.en: St. Cyril of Jerusalem As for that night, let darkness seize upon it; let it not rejoice among the days of the year, let it not come into the number of the months [6].

3.5.1.en: Fr. Hesychius distinguishes between two days: the day of disobedience that brought darkness upon us, and the day of the Savior in which He says: “This day is this scripture fulfilled in your ears” (Lk 4:21). The first day brought darkness and grief upon mankind, and the second is the joyful day of salvation in which the prophecy of the prophet Isaiah was fulfilled (Isa 61:1-2). For when we meet the Savior our joyful days of the Gospel are no longer compared with the days of gripping darkness that corrupts life. Therefore Job asked that the day of his birth in sin be cursed and utterly excluded and not counted among his days in the Lord.

3.5.2.en: * May that day and night be cursed, and let darkness carry them away, let it not enter into the number of the days of the months... May this day, the day of disobedience, not be counted among the benefits given to us through the Savior. May the grief (of the darkness) that comes from the day not be mixed with the blessings the Savior grants us, nor the curse corrupt them.

3.5.3.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem Lo, let that night be barren!

3.6.0.en: Let no shout be heard in it [7].

3.6.1.en: His ears could no longer bear the sound of music or shouting and rejoicing, because there is no place for joy in his depths. It is as though he had lost his hope for a time.

3.6.2.en: St. Augustine likens hope to an egg that carries within it a life which it presents through the warmth of tribulations and sufferings, for he says: [It is an egg, and not yet a (chick). It is covered with a shell, but do not look at it so; rather wait patiently, and put it in warmth and it will bring forth life. Press it.]

3.6.3.en: * Hope drives a person toward eternity, toward the future, in practical faith, and perseverance with joy and delight amid sufferings.

3.6.4.en: * Let us listen and rejoice in hope even if the present is a life not loved but endured, for you will have strength to bear all its trials.

3.6.5.en: * We rejoice in hope, looking to the coming rest; by this we walk with joy amid troubles.

3.6.6.en: St. Augustine * The person who does not look at what can be seen, but eagerly awaits what cannot be seen, rejoices in hope.

3.6.7.en: Origen * What is the hope of the Gospel but Christ? For He is our peace, who works all these things... and whoever does not believe in Christ loses everything.

3.6.8.en: * Hope is certainly like a strong rope let down from the heavens that helps our spirits, lifting whoever holds it firmly above this world and the trials of this evil life; but if a man is weak and lets go of this holy cord, he falls at once and is choked in the pit of evil.

3.6.9.en: * Nothing makes the soul so courageous and risk-loving as hope! And before our obtaining the things we hope for, it gives us a reward, which is: “patient in tribulation.” Before our obtaining the things to come, you enjoy in the present life a great good through trials, as you become a patient and proven man...

3.6.10.en: Love makes things easy, and the Spirit helps, and hope enlightens, and trials refine you, making you a proven one able to bear everything nobly; accompanying all this is a very great weapon, which is prayer.

3.6.11.en: St. John Chrysostom * Man's patience begets hope, and good hope glorifies man.

3.7.0.en: St. Evagrius Let them curse it that curse the day, who are ready to rouse up the dragon [8].

3.7.1.en: Just as the mourning women attend funerals and lament with the family and friends of the dead, so he reckoned the day of his birth a bitter funeral, and asks the cursers to come forward and share with him in cursing this day.

3.7.2.en: Some see that certain crocodile hunters used to curse crocodiles with the bitterest curses, hoping that the crocodile would become weak through their curses and incantations and they would gain mastery over it.

3.7.3.en: The Jesuit translation reads “Leviathan” instead of “dragon,” and as we shall see in its description in chapter forty-one that it applies to the crocodile, what is meant here are the curses that sorcerers and astrologers use to stir up Satan.

3.7.4.en: St. Gregory of Nazianzus warns us against comparing matters according to their size or weight. So we do not marvel if the Holy Spirit appeared in the form of a dove, and the Lord Christ was called a sheep [a lamb] (Isa 53:7) and a pearl (Mt 13:46) and dew [rain] (Ps 72:6), while the adversary was called a great mountain (Zech 4:7), and leviathan (Job 3:8; 40:20) and the king who lives in the waters (a). Let us not despise the Kingdom of Heaven because it was likened to a grain of mustard seed (Mt 13:31).

3.7.5.en: Let the stars of the evening thereof be dark.

3.8.0.en: Let it look for light, but have none; neither let it see the eyelashes of the morning [9]

3.8.1.en: *“Let the stars of its evening (its dusk) be dark... and let not Lucifer be seen rising” (Job 3:9) LXX. The stars of night are mentioned here with poor light, referring to the demons. For they take the form of an angel of light, but at the rising of the true Light (Jn 1:9) they become dark, and continue in their perversion.

3.8.2.en: This is what the text says: “Let it remain dark.” But they do not come to the light, since they cannot recover their tyranny.

3.8.3.en: Moreover, they will not see Lucifer standing, he of whom Isaiah said: [Lucifer, who rose in the morning] (Isa 14:12). After that he says [he was crushed to the earth] to indicate that he can no longer rise and return to his former dignity.

3.8.4.en: By his fall from heaven to earth he wanted to destroy man, but God gives the one who is not deceived authority to crush the deceiver under his feet, and to shatter him piece by piece.

3.8.5.en: But why does Job curse him?

3.8.6.en: For a good reason which he does not hide (which is what appears in the two verses [10-11]).

3.8.7.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem St. Augustine tells us of the defeat of the wicked devil, whose false light was extinguished by his killing the Lord Christ according to the flesh, the true Light, the Righteous One who dispels the darkness. He thought he could dispel Him as he shattered the first Adam, but behold, he shattered himself.

3.8.8.en: * What could be more righteous than reaching even the death of the Cross for the sake of righteousness?

3.8.9.en: And what work is greater in authority than the resurrection from the dead, and the ascension into heaven in the same body in which He was killed?

3.8.10.en: First the Righteous One conquered Satan, and afterward received authority!

3.8.11.en: The Righteous One triumphs because there is no sin in Him, and He died unjustly at the hands of Satan!

3.8.12.en: He receives authority, because He lived again after death, and will die no more...

3.8.13.en: Satan was defeated by his own victory...

3.8.14.en: By deceiving the first man he slew him, and by slaying the last Man he lost the first man from his net!

3.8.15.en: St. Augustine * In Holy Scripture the title “stars” is sometimes used for the righteousness of the saints shining in the darkness of this life, and sometimes for the vain appearance of hypocrites, who do every good thing for the praise of men. For if doers of good were not luminaries, Paul would not have said to his disciple: “in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation, among whom ye shine as lights in the world” (Phil 2:15).

3.8.16.en: Again, if there were not among (the members of the Church) those who seem outwardly to be walking uprightly, there would not be some who by their conduct receive honor from men, and John would not have seen the stars falling from heaven, when he said: [And his tail drew the third part of the stars of heaven, and did cast them to the earth] (Rev 12:4).

3.8.17.en: * The eyelashes of the morning [the rising of the dawn] is the beginning of the Church in the light, where the wicked cannot be seen, for they are shut in and compelled to descend into darkness through the weight of their evil works, so that they do not see the just Judge. Thus it was truly said by the prophet: Let the wicked be taken away from the way, that he behold not the glory of God (Isa 26:10) LXX.

3.9.0.en: Because it shut not up the doors of my mother's womb, nor hid sorrow from mine eyes [10].

3.9.1.en: His wisdom failed him, so Job desired something extremely cruel, namely that his mother had given birth to him before the appointed time, so that her womb would open and he would come out a stillborn, and she herself would be exposed to danger and even death. A very painful picture because of complaining!

3.9.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us a wonderful symbolic interpretation of this phrase, where he sees the believer returning to the first parents while in Paradise as in a mother's womb, and he wished to be born there and that the gates of Paradise not be opened to drive him out by the serpent. He says that the serpent opened the mouth of this womb for man to come out of the joyful garden, and to live in the valley of death. He desires that the door of the first Paradise had remained closed so that humanity would be born and multiply in heavenly, joyful gladness.

3.10.s.en: 2. He wonders why he did not die and go to the grave as soon as he was born

3.10.0.en: He wished he had died immediately after his birth, for he believes that this would have been better for him, for he would then be with “kings and counselors of the earth,” in rest and quiet in the grave. For death is better than life.

3.11.s.en: 3. The song of death and its sweetness

3.11.0.en: 11 Why died I not from the womb? why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? 12 Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck? 13 For now should I have lain still and been quiet, I should have slept: then had I been at rest, 14 With kings and counsellors of the earth, which built pyramids for themselves; 15 Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver: 16 Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light. 17 There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest. 18 There the prisoners are at ease together; they hear not the voice of the taskmaster. 19 The small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master.

3.11.1.en: Offering a lament, desiring that he had died in the womb, he looked at his life with its pains and calamities and found death sweet, offering a poem about death that is sweeter than temporal life, so to speak. He saw in the abyss deliverance from what he suffers on earth.

3.11.2.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) offers us at length a symbolic interpretation of the song of death and its sweetness, seeing in Job that he desired to die in the womb, that is, with his parents Adam and Eve in Paradise before going out to the world that lies in the Evil One, as we saw. And he sees in his meeting in the grave with the kings and counselors of the earth a meeting with the giants of faith and the spiritual leaders, where all rest in one eternal life, in which there is no one groaning or suffering, nor any small one envying a great one [The prisoners are at ease, they hear not the voice of the taskmaster; the small and great are there, and the servant is free from his master] (Job 3:18-19).

3.11.3.en: Why died I not from the womb?

3.11.4.en: Why did I not give up the ghost when I came out of the belly? [11]

3.11.5.en: Perhaps Job realized his mistake when he desired that his mother be endangered by his coming out stillborn before the time of his birth; he returned to correct the matter, and desired that he had been born and died immediately after coming out of his mother's womb.

3.11.6.en: Job looked at life from his birth as a curse and calamity to him, and reckoned death the greatest blessing that could have come upon him. In contrast to this the prophet Jeremiah in the midst of his bitter lament offers a hymn of thanks to God for “the gift of life,” saying: [It is of the LORD's mercies that we did not die from the womb, and were not annihilated] (Lam 3:22).

3.11.7.en: It is told in a fable that an old man was very tired from carrying something heavy, so he threw the load on the ground, and in his despair he called upon Death. When Death came and asked him what he wanted, supposing he was asking to take his soul and die, he was surprised when he said: “I beg you to help me carry my heavy load.”

3.11.8.en: Job offered us a lament in which he sings of his love of early death from the moments of his birth and praises the grave in it. It is as though death and the grave had become his intimate friends. But when the Lord Christ came by His own will and authority to death and the grave, turning it into a joyful song, it is sung not by the despairing but by those full of hope in the heavenly things, who seek fellowship in eternal glory, and who long to meet their heavenly friends, sharing with them their praises.

3.11.9.en: Through Christ Jesus the Crucified, the Giver of resurrection, we sing: “For whether we live, we live unto the Lord; and whether we die, we die unto the Lord: whether we live therefore, or die, we are the Lord's” (Rom 14:8).

3.12.0.en: Why did the knees prevent me? or why the breasts that I should suck? [12]

3.12.1.en: Pope Gregory (the Great) rejects the literal interpretation of the two verses [11-12], looking at the blessed Job who was given such lofty spiritual knowledge, and offered praises to the Judge in his depths, and cannot desire to have died by miscarriage, or immediately at his birth. Rather he sees in these two verses the righteous Job lamenting either his committing sin in the heart or practicing it in deed. He says there are four ways of committing sin in the heart, and four similar ways of committing it in deed, and he desires that it had perished in its stages before reaching its full maturity. These four stages are:

3.12.2.en: A. Its conception in the womb: this is the first stage where it begins in the heart by the presentation of the suggestion, and in deed the practice takes place secretly.

3.12.3.en: B. Its coming out of the womb or its birth: this is the second stage, where the suggestion turns into delight in the heart, and in deed it turns from secret practice into open practice before the eyes of people without shame.

3.12.4.en: C. The knees' receiving it: the third stage, where it turns from delight of the heart into inward consent and acceptance. And in deed it turns from open practice into a habit to which the sinner is enslaved.

3.12.5.en: D. Suckling from the breast: the last stage, where it turns from acceptance of sin into defense of what the sinner commits, as though he had not sinned. And in deed it turns from habit into full maturity in the practice of sin.

3.12.6.en: The four stages: sin in the heart; sin in deed. (1) Conception in the womb: the suggestion of sin; committing it secretly. (2) Coming out of the womb or its birth: delight of the heart; committing it openly without shame. (3) The support of the knees: inward consent of the heart; turning it into a habit. (4) The nourishing of the child by the breasts or suckling: defense of the error; its growth and maturity. Pope Gregory concludes this discussion by saying:

3.12.7.en: [It is fitting for us also to know that the ways (the first three stages) can be corrected easily... but the fourth (stage) cannot be corrected except with difficulty.

3.12.8.en: Thus our Savior raised the girl in the house, and the young man outside the gate, but Lazarus He raised in the tomb. For he who commits sin secretly is like a dead person laid in the house. But he who commits sin openly has been carried outside the gate, committing sin shamelessly in the open. And he who commits sin once and many times under the pressure of habit has fallen into the heap of the tomb.

3.12.9.en: And yet the Savior in His mercy restores all of these to life, for grace often shines in this case with its light upon the dead, not only through hidden sins but also upon him who practices them openly, and who falls under the pressure of habit...

3.12.10.en: But our Savior does not raise those of the fourth way to life. Truly it is hard for the one who continues in his evil habit, holding fast to the tongues of flatterers (defending the error), to be healed of the death of the soul. Of this it was said: “Let the dead bury their dead” (Lk 9:60). For the dead bury their dead.]

3.12.11.en: Thus Pope Gregory sees in the fourth stage of sin, which is the defense of the error and covering it, its arrival at maturity and the impossibility of rising from its death until the sinner confesses his sin and does not justify his error or give himself an excuse as both Adam and Eve did.

3.12.12.en: For now should I have lain still and been quiet,

3.13.0.en: Then I should have slept and been at rest [13]

3.13.1.en: Pope Gregory offers us a justification for the bitterness of Job's soul. He looks at what man could have attained had sin not entered into his life. He says:

3.13.2.en: [Man was placed in Paradise, and bonds of love were attached to him that he might follow his Creator in obedience; thus he could have been transferred one day to the heavenly city of the angels even without the death of the body. For he was created immortal in a manner by which he could die if he sinned, and so become mortal. But if he had not sinned he could have remained without death, and in full freedom receive the blessedness of a world in which there is no possibility of error or of death.

3.13.3.en: Since the time of redemption the elect are sent through the death of their bodies to the very place which the first parents ought to have reached without the death of the body had they remained steadfast in what they were created. Thus man would have remained “lying down and at rest,” reaching his eternal city in rest. He would have found in it a place of rest and quiet from the tumult of human weakness...

3.13.4.en: This quiet of peace man enjoyed when he was created and received freedom of will to face his enemy. But when he submitted to him by his own will, immediately human weakness was found settled in him. For although he was created by his Creator in a state of quiet full of peace, as soon as he bowed under his enemy by his will he fell under the tumult of war. The suggestions of the flesh itself became a kind of cry against the rest of the mind, something man did not know before the disobedience, because it did not exist, and he bound himself to his sins, so that it came to serve him in matters against his will, and he suffered from the tumult of thought, as the flesh wrestles against the spirit.]

3.13.5.en: *Rejoicing in God's creation is desirable; that a person become a man (mature) receiving the image of God, this is happiness. But loitering in defiled life, and being captivated for the sake of many people, this the righteous hate.

3.14.0.en: Fr. Hesychius of Jerusalem With kings and counsellors of the earth, which built pyramids for themselves [14]

3.14.1.en: Job reckoned death a rest with the kings of the earth and their counselors, those who wanted to immortalize their memory by building the pyramids and huge, luxurious tombs, but no one is any longer able to distinguish between their dust. The pyramids and gold and silver and all they left behind no longer represent anything.

3.14.2.en: Pope Gregory sees that the kings here are the angelic spirits who devoted their energy to serving the Creator of all beings subject to them. They are also called counselors because they give counsel to the spiritual world, where they unite us to themselves as partners with them in the Kingdom.

3.15.0.en: Or with princes that had gold, who filled their houses with silver [15]

3.15.1.en: It was the custom of kings and great men to place gold and silver in their tombs as a kind of honor even after death, and perhaps lest their corpses mingle with the corpses of the poor. But death does not distinguish between great and lowly, rich and poor, master and servant. As the wise man says: [The rich and poor meet together] (Prov 22:2).

3.15.2.en: Pope Gregory sees that the princes are the leaders of the holy Church who fill their houses with the word of God, the gold refined by fire (Ps 12:6).

3.16.0.en: Or as an hidden untimely birth I had not been; as infants which never saw light [16].

3.16.1.en: In the grave after the dissolution of the body there is no one who can distinguish between the dust of a king or a great man or a buried stillborn who never came out to life in the world. Job sees that the fetuses that died before seeing the light of life are in a happier rest than he is in, for he desires sleep to rest and does not find it.

3.16.2.en: Job desired sleep even as a fetus that never saw the world, and did not realize that true rest is in Christ Jesus, in whom alone we sleep, that is, are buried with Him, to rise to eternal life in surpassing glory beyond expression.

3.16.3.en: Pope Gregory sees that the buried stillborn who rest are the elect from the beginning of the world who lived before salvation and yet died to the world, those who did not have the two tablets of the Law, so they died as in the womb, and feared God through the natural law. They believed that the Intercessor was coming, so they strove as they could; they mortified themselves to pleasures, and kept the concepts which the Law had not yet recorded. This period before the Law presented us our fathers dead for this life; they were like fetuses that died in the womb.

3.16.4.en: This Pope offered us examples of the stillborn:

3.16.5.en: A. Abel: of whom we do not read that he resisted his brother when he killed him.

3.16.6.en: B. Enoch: who was commended, and walked with God and was translated.

3.16.7.en: C. Noah: who by divine judgment became the only one (with his family) alive.

3.16.8.en: D. Abraham: a pilgrim in the world, because he is the friend of God.

3.16.9.en: E. Isaac: a pilgrim with his physical eyes weak from old age, he did not see present things, but was enlightened by the spirit of prophecy, to see the things to come with extraordinary insight.

3.16.10.en: F. Jacob: in humility he fled from the wrath of his brother, and by his gentleness conquered him. He was fruitful in his offspring, and more fruitful in the riches of the Spirit, so he bound his offspring with the bonds of prophecy.

3.17.0.en: There the wicked cease from troubling; and there the weary be at rest [17].

3.17.1.en: Death puts a final end to the injustice of the wicked who do not cease to resist the truth and persecute the children of God, for death ended what Herod, persecutor of the Church, did (Acts 12:1-6, 23). And death grants true rest to those who bore persecution with thanksgiving for God's sake. “Write, Blessed are the dead which die in the Lord from henceforth: Yea, saith the Spirit, that they may rest from their labours; and their works do follow them” (Rev 14:13). “The righteous is taken away from the evil to come. He shall enter into peace: they shall rest in their beds” (Isa 57:1-2).

3.17.2.en: * Then comes praise to death, and thanks to it, for it takes some away from evil, and others are freed from their misery, those who find in it a refuge against their evils, and those who find in it an obstacle that restrains their malice.

3.17.3.en: St. John Chrysostom The prisoners are at ease together.

3.18.0.en: They hear not the voice of the taskmaster [18].

3.18.1.en: Captives often desire death to rest from humiliation. Samson preferred to die with all those who mocked him rather than live grinding “in the prison house” (Judg 16:21).

3.18.2.en: * Death abolishes everything. Not only is there no longer a possibility of supporting evil, but not even the mere sound of evil reaches the ears anymore.

3.19.0.en: St. John Chrysostom The small and great are there; and the servant is free from his master [19].

3.19.1.en: By death the taskmaster and the one under forced labor become equal, the great with the small. All lie together in the grave which makes no distinction between this one and that.

3.19.2.en: * No one can escape its authority, neither slave nor free. All human things perish with death: wealth as well as honor. The inequality in this present life is enormous. Great is the freedom after our departure there.

3.19.3.en: St. John Chrysostom * I add: “and the servant is free from his master,” for it is written: “Whosoever committeth sin is the servant of sin” (Jn 8:34)... In this present life the servant indeed flees from his master, but he is not free from him... But there the servant is free from his master. There is no longer any doubt there about the forgiveness of sin, when the remembrance of sin no longer condemns the soul. The soul becomes secure, so the conscience is not terrified by a sense of guilt, but rejoices in forgiveness and its enjoyment of freedom, Pope Gregory (the Great)

3.19.4.en: * Death leads to itself slaves and their masters, and there the masters are not honored more than their servants.

3.20.s.en: 4. The riddle of the survival of those who desire death

3.20.0.en: 20 Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul; 21 Which long for death, but it cometh not; and dig for it more than for hid treasures; 22 Which rejoice exceedingly, and are glad, when they can find the grave? 23 To a man whose way is hid from him, and whom God hath hedged in? 24 For my sighing cometh like my bread, and my roarings are poured out like the waters. 25 For I was greatly terrified, and it came upon me, and that which I dreaded came upon me. 26 I was not in safety, neither had I rest, neither was I quiet; yet trouble came.

3.20.1.en: In astonishment Job looks at those who desire death and do not find it, for God hedges them about as with a fence, that they may live a life of pain without realizing God's plan for them.

3.20.2.en: When Job found that it did not help to wish that he had not been born, or had died as soon as he was born, we see him here complaining that his life continued remaining without being cut off; he cried out because of the long period of trial. He justified his intense desire for death with the following: 1- He felt constantly weary amid his severe afflictions, which seemed as though they would continue. 2- Even in the days of his former prosperity he was always afraid of troubles, and therefore never felt at rest, and therefore said [I was not in safety, nor quiet, nor had I rest].

3.20.3.en: With the testimony of James the Apostle to Job, “Ye have heard of the patience of Job” (Jas 5:11), and with his endurance of all these trials without sinning, and with what he saw on the faces of his friends of intense sorrow for his condition, he opened his mouth to speak. He began to complain that he was born, and that he did not die when he was born, and that his life was prolonged in his affliction. He had been patient for a long time, but he could no longer bear it. For however great a man's patience, let him realize that he is weak and liable to fall. It is as though the Book warns us with the Apostle Paul: [Let him that thinketh he standeth take heed lest he fall] (1 Cor 10:12).

3.20.4.en: Wherefore is light given to him that is in misery, and life unto the bitter in soul? [20]

3.20.5.en: Job complains here that his life continued and did not cease. He hastens death, welcoming its coming. Although light is a good gift, in the midst of his bitterness he reckoned this light to increase his misery. The candle of his life was given to him so that he might see the misery he was in, and it would have been better for him to have no such light.

3.20.6.en: * All the righteous are in sorrows in this life (Ps 34:19), those of whom it was said: “we must through much tribulation enter into the kingdom of God” (Acts 14:22). [They have eaten ashes like bread, and mingled their drink with weeping] (cf. Ps 102:9). They desire to pass through the trials here, giving thanks for these means. Thus they are in sorrow like David declaring with such phrases: “All the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears” (Ps 6:6).
